headline: CAT BURGLARS
text:
NIGHT PROWLERS CAUGHT.

HEIGHT OF EFFRONTERY

With the near approach of Chinese New Year, the activities of cat burglars were "shewn in two cases which came up at the Central Magistracy this morning." A young Chinese who desired a change from his business of bottling picked crabs was one of the offenders. He had applied for a position as a police recruit, and was to have been given a trial. Pending his appointment he had scaled a drain pipe at a Queen's Road dentist's shop during night time and appropriated four articles of clothing. Wearing a new overcoat included in the "swag" and trying to fraternise with the detectives, he was suspected and put through a search. Pawn tickets for the other stolen clothing were found in his pocket.

With a crestfallen air, the offender awaited a sentence of four months' hard labour imposed by the Magistrate.

The story of a chase in the area near "Paddy's Market" was given in evidence before Major C. Willson when another offender was caught without accomplishing his object. Startled by a tap at the door of a house which he entered last night, the thief was poticed by an Indian constable to be scaling a wall. His attempted escape by jumping into a courtyard failed, as two other constables kept on his heels and caught him.

In this case the sentence was three months' hard labour.

headline: SHIPS IN CANTON.
text:
FRENCH SHIP REPORTED DETAINED:

KINSHAN) PTRED AT

The French steamer "Limchow" is reported to have been detained (according to a cable to the "Wah Tsz Yat Po") at Canton, while on a trip there from Haiphong. No details have been given.

The "Limchow" was once a regular caller at Hongkong but has not been here for some time. She is of 1,416 tons (registered) and was built in Hamburg in 1894. Formerly she was known as the "Songma" and the "Thelka Boklen."

Whilst anchored in the stream at Canton on Saturday evening, the Steamboat Co.'s s.s. "Kinshan" was fired at by river pickets who endeavoured to intercept sampans with fish.

Hitherto the pickets had refrained from firing when in range of the river steamers. The "Kinshan's" woodwork shows marks of where the bullets struck, ostensibly after missing the sampans breaking through the strikers' cordon.

Frequently the state of disorder among lawless testers who have their hearts in stummi. Canton Road provided a scrap between the police and a hostile crowd of Chinese last night. Stones and other misiles were freely used in attack on the police, who in fire and to defend themselves with revolvers.

Organised gambling is in a flourishing state among the inhabitants in this area. Only recently the police broke up a gambling party which was riding business with a Chinese orchestra in attendance, and several convictions resulted in the Rowston Court.

The array which took place at 9 p.m. yesterday was the outcome of a similar raid carried out by Detective Sub-Inspector Andrew assisted by five Chinese detectives. The gamblers were surrounded in the ground floor of a house. Fifteen were arrested and a sum of $15.80 was taken together with other evidence.

The prisoners, all handcuffed, were taken to the street. Here the police encountered a hostile mob numbering about 300 Chinese who made a sudden onslaught and rescued thirteen of the arrested persons. The police were out-numbered and were obliged to retreat. Three detectives were struck by missiles. Sub-Inspector Andrew was also hit by a stone in the shin. The police had to make judicious use of their revolvers. A rebounding bullet wounded a Chinese who was later picked up and sent to the hospital.

The two men who were not rescued by their staff were charged before Mr. E. Hamilton at the Kowloon Magasacy the north by with being concerned in the gambling. Evidence of the raid was given by Sub-Inspector Andrew and each man was fined $25.

headline: WEE DRAPPIE.
text:
TEMPTING POWER OVER A COOLIE

Stealing a bottle of whisky from the s.s. "Fulda" after breaking a case, a cargo coolie swallowed half of it and was caught when he was getting away with the bottle under his arm.

Mr. R. A. D. Forrest, who had the offender before him at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning, accepted counsel's plea that there was temptation and bound the man over.

headline: HEROISM AT SEA.
text:
KING'S MESSAGE TO U.S. PRESIDENT

The gallantry displayed by Captain Fried and the crew of the "President Roosevelt" in reaching the crew of the British steamer "Antinoe" has aroused the greatest admiration here.

His Majesty King George, in a message to President Coolidge, says that the heroism shown under such terrible conditions has greatly moved him, and adds:

"In expressing my thankfulness and admiration for this splendid example of skill and gallantry I know that I am only voicing the feelings of all British hearts. At the same time we grieve at the loss of those men who nobly sacrificed their lives, and I would ask you to assure the bereaved families of my heartfelt sympathy." President Coolidge, in his reply,

“The event is but another illustration of the heroism and gallantry which have characterised alike the mariners of the United States and Great Britain, and, while regretting the occasion therefor, I rejoice that American sailors have been able to help those of Great Britain.”

At Queenstown last night the President Roosevelt was greeted on arrival by a crowd of many thousands and the Lord Mayor of Cork expressed to Captain Fried the admiration felt by the people of the Irish State.

Reception at Plymouth. When the “President Roosevelt reached Plymouth to-day a great crowd lined the quays and the sea-front. The Mayor of Plymouth, the Chairman of the Chamber of Commerce, and President of the Tobacco organisations were present. The Admiralty and the British Navy were represented by Captain Goldsmith, of the warship “Douglas” and the Board of Trade by Captain King.

In reply to congratulatory speeches, expressing deep admiration, and appreciation, Captain Fried, on behalf of his officers and crew, insisted modestly that any other ship able to cope with an emergency would have done the same as his vessel.

Captain Goldsmith specially conveyed to Captain Fried the Admiral's warmest congratulations on his magnificent seamanship, which rendered possible the rescue of the crew of the "Antinoe," and of the great gallantry displayed by the officers and men concerned in the rescue.

Sympathy in the loss of two of the crew of the “President Roosevelt” during this hazardous undertaking was also officially expressed.

headline: TRAFFIC LAW.
text:
MOTOR DRIVER'S LAPSE

AN ACCIDENT SEQUEL

：

More than half a dozen motor accidents attended with injuries to persons were reported during the week-end.

In one of the accidents a Sanitary Board coolie was injured in the leg at Pokfulam Roads Owing to the wet state of the road, the motorcar which struck him sided and collided with a stationary car.

Limping; but satisfied with a gratuity of $2, a coolie walked away after he was knocked down by Mr. Douglas Wong, a motor cyclist.

Trivial though the accidents were, a Chinese motor driver failed to report that he had caused both 'damage' and injury to a ricsha and its puller early yesterday morning at Queen's Road West. The offender was traced and at the Central Magistracy this morning he was fined $100, or six weeks' hard labour. He was further ordered to pay $40 as compensation.

The “Antinoe’s” Captain, before disembarking, handed letters to Captain Fried and the “President Roosevelt’s” chief, officer who manned the rescue boats, expressing heartfelt gratitude on behalf of himself, his officers, and his crew, saying: “You have indeed given us back our lives.”

Some public recognition of the gallantry of the Captain and crew of the "President Roosevelt" was expressed in an informal gathering in the President Roosevelt's saloon, speeches being made by the Mayor of Plymouth and the Chairman of the Plymouth Chamber of Commerce.

The wife of the “Antinoe’s” captain, ardently thanked Captain Fried who replied, “It’s nothing; I’ve a good name sailors do for one another.”

headline: EDUCATION
text:
FORMER HONGKONG MAN SPEAKS OUT.

COLLEGE DOMINATION.

Dr. John Stuart-Thomson, formerly of Hongkong, contributes a leading article on University life and education to the World Travel Gazette that is making some stir in the international education world. It recommends the ancient English custom in academic things of letting the colleges be managed by the faculties and students rather than be academically and athletically dominated by rich donors who are seeking advertisement, propaganda or some other private advantage.

Dr. Thomson for three years was manager at Hongkong of the Pacific Mail and Toyo Kisen Kaisha S.S. Co.'s office in Queen's Building, living at the Peak Hotel and Hongkong Club. During that time he contributed poems to Chamber's Journal, Edinburgh, the most famous being "The Alien's Farewell," December 1, 1902 and "The Alien's Return" 1904.

Dr. Thomson is a well-known constitutional and civic-zoning authority and Far East Explorer and is being run by the New Jersey press for U.S. Senator; The article makes him popular with the students and the faculties though it means an popular with the exploiters of colleges. A former college athlete himself (quarterback, track, lacrosse) he is opposed to the present professionalized athletic system, which he says is too much a spectacle for non-athletes and non-col觉者.

headline: KOWLOON RIOT.
text:
ALLEGED RINGLEADER ARRESTED

FURTHER DEVELOPMENTS?

Alleged to be the ringleader of the riot in Yaumati on Sunday night when the Police had to open fire, a Chinese came up before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning and was remanded to await further developments.

Three men have been arrested in a tea-house, it is reported, and the defendant is believed to have been one of these.

Charges of abetting the release of prisoners in custody and obstructing the police were preferred against him.

headline: FALSE FRIENDSHIP
text:
LODGEIR DECAMPS WITH CLOTHING

CHINESE JAILED:

"You take advantage of his hospitality and steal his property," was the remark made by Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning when he imposed sentence of four weeks' hard labour on a Chinese who had stolen some clothing.

Divisional Inspector Ogr. said that the day after the theft the defendant and complainant accidentally met in the street. Defendant made an attempt to escape, but was caught after a chase.

headline: A SINCERE TRIBUTE.
text:
Before Captain Tose left the "President Roosevelt" yesterday, he handed the commander of the liner a message, expressing his heartfelt gratitude and stating:

"Your splendid determination to save us at all costs, even at the cost of your brave men, filled us with the deepest thankfulness. We shall never forget your noble spirited sacrifice and your devotion to the highest instincts of humanity. Your superb handling of your ship in extreme difficulty merits our lasting praise as seamen."

Precisely similar installations will be fitted in her sister ship "Alcantara" and in the new Union Castle liner "Carnarvon Castle" recently launched.

There will be no difficulty in recognising this tric wherever they may be, owing to the two large but very low funnels with which they are provided.

headline: RAILWAY WAGES.
text:
DEMAND OF AMERICAN EMPLOYEES

A DOLLAR A DAY MORE.

The drivers and conductors of the Eastern States Railways have requested the employers to agree by March 2, to an increase in pay of a dollar per day.

headline: MR. WU ANSWERED. / GOVERNOR ON CANTON'S DUTY.
text:
This morning's meeting of the Legislative Council was noteworthy in that before the agenda business, H.E. the Governor made statement with regard to the present boycott.

The boycott had been characterized by flagrant violations of treaty rights which it was, the duty of the Canton Government to require the Strike Committee to put an end to, he stated. Their failure to do this throws grave doubt upon its professed sincerity in desiring an early settlement, he added.

The activities of emissaries to incite a strike in Hongkong was subject of reference. It was indicated that drastic steps would taken against such if the attempts were not immediately dissued.

Following is the full text of His Excellency the Governor's remarks. His Excellency said: Your Excellency and gentlemen, I regret to inform the Council that the anti-British boycott in the Kuang-tung Province still continues in spite of the efforts made by the Hongkong Government to negotiate a settlement. This boycott originated from a strike, which according to a communiqué issued last month by the Canton Commissioner of Foreign Affairs "was instituted by Hongkong workers, not for economic reasons, but as a protest against the British Government," and which is claimed in a resolution recently passed at a special meeting of the Four Chambers of Commerce in Canton to be "a patriotic demonstration of the people for the honour of the country."

“Unlawful Tyranny.” But, if this be so, how came it that the Canton Strike Committee was obliged from the outset to maintain thousands of strike pickets in Canton and elsewhere, in order to prevent the Hongkong workers from returning to their employment in this Colony? And, why is it that the strike is now to all in-tents and purpose? Is it thing of the past, and that, in spite of every means of intimidation, employed by the Canton Strike Committee, almost the whole body of Hongkong labourers is now again at work? Moreover, is it not certain that the anti-British boycott in the Kuang-tung Province would not last another day but for the unlawful tyranny imposed upon the Cantonese people by the Canton Strike Committee? The Strike Committee can easily put this matter to the tust. Let it withdraw all the strike pickets, abstain from all foreible interference with trade in the Kuang-tung Province, and note the result.

Kuang-tung Province, and we are persuaded that the great mass of the Cantonese people are still, as they used to be, ready and willing to trade with us in the most amicable manner to our mutual advantage. (Applause). Only the unlawful activities of the Canton Strike Committee, instigated by Bolshevik intrigue, prevent the resumption of normal relations between Canton and Hongkong on the old, familiar footing. We expect and require the Canton Government to put an end to these illegalities. We hold the Canton Government to be principals in this matter. I also wish it to be clearly understood that the Hongkong Government will never agree in principle to strike pay or to compensation for non-reinstatement of labourers. (Applause).

I must close with a word of warning. It has been brought to my notice that attempts have recently been made in Hongkong by emissaries of the Canton Strike Committee to incite a new strike. If these attempts are not immediately discontinued, the Hongkong Government will take drastic steps to put in stop to them; and should any labourers be so ill-advised as to desert their employment—a contingency which I believe to be remote—I am confident that the whole community can be depended upon to rise to the occasion, as it has done before. (Applause). The emergency organisation, which did such splendid work last year, is still in being and is ready to be put in force at any moment, should circumstances demand its use. We are determined to give full protection to the people of Hongkong, and to put down with a firm hand any conspiracy to intimidate or otherwise to cause, trouble among labourers and merchants in this Colony. In all necessary measures to that end, I know that I can rely upon the wholehearted support of this Council. (Applause).

headline: Government As Principals.
parent_headline: MR. WU ANSWERED. / GOVERNOR ON CANTON'S DUTY.
text:
The Canton Commissioner of Foreign Affairs argues in his communique that the principals in this matter are the Canton Strike Committee on the one side and the Hongkong Government on the other and that, therefore, a settlement should be negotiated by the Hongkong Government with the Strike Committee. I desire to make it perfectly clear that the Hongkong Government cannot negotiate in Canton with any but the Canton Government. Moreover, the boycott maintained by the Canton Strike Committee to the detriment chiefly of their own fellow countrymen is characterized by flagrant violations of treaty rights, which it is the duty of the Canton Government to respect. Consequently it is the duty of the Canton Government to require the Canton Strike Committee to put an end to such illegalities. The Canton Government has not yet done this, and its failure to do so throws grave doubt upon its professed sincerity in desiring an early settlement, and makes it difficult to give credence to the statement in the communique of the Canton Commissioner of Foreign Affairs that "the Government at Canton, though deeply interested in the issue, was not a party to the strike or boycott." The Canton Government is, of course, responsible for the maintenance of law and order in the areas under its administration; and in as much as it has left unchecked and unpunished the illegal activities of the Canton Strike Committee directed against this Colony, it is liable for all losses incurred owing to such illegal activities. (Applause).

The Hongkong Government desires an honourable and a lasting settlement of the boycott, and remains prepared to negotiate such a settlement with the Canton Government. We in this Colony are animated by the friendliest feelings towards our neighbours in the

headline: Members' Approval.
parent_headline: MR. WU ANSWERED. / GOVERNOR ON CANTON'S DUTY.
text:
ness before Council, the Hon. Sir Henry Pollock said:— As this is the first meeting of the Council which has taken place since the New Year Honours List, I desire, Sir, on behalf of my Official colleagues to tender to Your Excellency, our most hearty congratulations on having bestowed on you by His Majesty the King, the Knight Commandership of the Most Distinguished Order of Saint Michael and Saint George, (Applause).

This is an honour, Sir, in the normal course of things, bestowed on Governors of this Colony, but in this particular case, Sir, we feel specially inclined to congratulate you when we recollect that you started your career as a civil servant here in Hongkong and that in fact, of your total period of service with the Colonial Service, including your time in other places, more than half of your time was in the service of this Colony.

Therefore, Sir, we feel it is an honour not only to you but to this Colony that you should have received this recognition of your services. Arriving amongst us, Sir, at a time when matters were considerably strained, as they still are, between the Hongkong and Canton Governments, you have this morning given a manly and straightforward declaration of the attitude and policy of this Government in the matter of the boycott. I can assure you, from my knowledge of public opinion in this Colony, that these straightforward words of yours will meet with most hearty approval. From the members of this community. (Applause).

In conclusion, Sir Henry congratulated his Honourable colleague, the senior Unofficial Chinese member, Sir Shou Son Chow, on the honour bestowed on

him. As was probably known to most members, Sir Shou Son Chow could claim a very remote connection with this Colony because, even before the British took it over, he had ancestors residing in the village of Stanley.

Henry, Sir Shou Son Chow has had a very distinguished career. For many years he held important posts under the Imperial Government of China and filled these posts with great ability. We all of us know that he has put a great deal of unpaid public duty into the forwarding of the welfare of this Colony by sitting on numerous and important Committees here affecting the Chinese. The Council has had the pleasure of his presence here on the Council Board for over four years past and has grown to value his advice as a member of the Council. During the last seven months, in particular, added Sir Henry, we feel not only indebted to Sir Shou Son Chow but also to his Chinese colleague for the excellent work put in by them in the period of unrest existing. We are, perhaps, in a position more fully to appreciate than the general public, the enormous value of the unstinted efforts of the Chinese members of this Council during the period to which I have referred. I may safely say that the honour conferred on him has met with the very warm approval of all sections and races of this community.

In reply, His Excellency thanked Sir Henry very sincerely for the manner in which he had congratulated him on the honour bestowed on him by His Mapesty the King. He would like to convey to the Council, and, through them, to the whole community, his warmest thanks for the welcome given to him on his return to this Colony. It had been of the greatest possible encouragement to him in discharging the very heavy and anxious duties devolving on him as Governor. For this he was most grateful. Sir Shou, Son Chew also suitably replied.

headline: SOMERSET MAUGHAM
text:
"PAINTED VEIL" AUTHOR IN HONGKONG.

"UNNECESSARY FUSS."

His Characters As "Purely Imaginary"

The coldest man in Hongkong today is probably Mr. Somerset Maugham, playwright, novelist and traveller, best known in Hongkong as author of "The Painted Vell", a book which was given much free advertisement owing to the holding up of the first edition and the changing of the scenes from Hongkong to an imaginary place.

Having undertaken the trip from Manila to Hongkong at a moment's notice through force of circumstances, Mr. Naugham has only his summer clothes and a topee with him. "You find me rather chilly," he remarked to a "China Mail" representative who interviewed him this morning.

Mr. Maugham was to catch a boat at Manila to take him direct to Saigon but he missed it and has come to Hongkong in order to make a connection with the U.S. "Hanoi" which leaves to-morrow. He is collecting material for a volume of short stories about Malaya. Borneo and the Far East.

Asked if Hongkong would figure in these stories, Mr Maugham shook his head. A novelist was always on the look out for subject matter, however, he added, and something might strike him as worth noting here. With regard to "The Fainted Veil," a subject which the "China Mail" representative introduced, Mr. Maugham said that a lot of unnecessary fuss had been made. The plot and characters were purely imaginary.

As to the general manner of his approach of subjects and places for his books and descriptions, Mr. Maugham said that he always made it a practice to become acquainted with places before he wrote about them. His stories were not intended to apply to personalities literally. Experiences he heard of in different places might provide an idea but real life was never complete enough for a satisfactory story to be made of it. “In all stories it might be said that perhaps fifteen per cent. is life and the rest invention,” added Mr. Maugham. “Any sensible novelist who wanted to put scenes into his story, however, should stop long enough to get acquainted with such details as he wanted to use. “I find a certain interest in studying exotic surroundings and customs and the effect on the characters of the white people who live among them.”

headline: COURT GLIMPSES / A FALLING OFF IN CRIME
text:
HAWKERS' LUCK.

With the relaxation in the law against unlicensed hawkers and the general falling off in crime, there were few cases in the Police Courts this morning.

Forbidden Newspapers:

An employee of the "Tai Kwong Po" newspaper was charged before Mr. R. E. Lindsell with the possession of 21 different newspapers published in Canton, the circulation of which is forbidden in the Colony. Defendant was arrested as he was leaving the wharf after boarding the S.S. "Lungshan" which arrived from Canton on Tuesday afternoon.

Detective-Sub-Inspector Shannon explained the delay in bringing the defendant before His Worship by stating that he had to submit the newspapers to the Secretary for Chinese Affairs to have translations taken.

Defendant said that he was only carrying out the instructions of his master to receive the newspapers from a man on board. His Worship agreed there was some truth in this story, and remained defendant on $200 bail until Monday, pending enquiries as to why the "Tai Kwong Po" imported the papers.

A Chinese youngster was charged before Major C. Willson with the theft of $20 from Mr. H. Pritham, of On-Hing Terrace.

Defendant said that he found the money on the ground while doing some odd jobs in complainant's house and he placed the notes inside his shoe.

The Magistrate imposed sentence of three weeks' hard labour and eight strokes of the birch.

On a charge of unlawful possession of a quantity of cloth,g and an electric fan, two Chinese explained that the articles were given to them in lieu of wages by the master of a Chinese firm which had closed down. This was later borne out by the wife of the man.

Sergeant Brittain said that the master was the debtor in a bank-ruptcy case at the Summary Court yesterday, who is believed to have absconded.

Defendants were discharged.

C. T. French, wireless watchman of the s.s. "Delta," was again before the Kowloon Magistrate this morning to receive sentence in a charge of theft of passengers' belongings which was proved against him on Wednesday.

The Magistrate said he did not wish to imprisonment on account of his youth, and ordered him to sign a bond for good behaviour in a sum of $250.

headline: TYPHOON RECALLED.
text:
The foregoing refers to the disastrous typhoon of August 18, 1923, which resulted in the loss of the Indo-China s.s. "Loong Sang," which, founded with loss of many lives after being swept away from her mooring. One of the British submarines—the L9—went down near Queen's Pier, the crew being saved by the Japanese steamer "Ginyo Maru." The liners "Empress of Australia" and "Andre Lebon" were in great danger for a time owing to their anchors dragging.

The officers and crew of the 5.s. "Egremont Castle," which was dragging her anchors near Stonecutter's Island, performed fine heroic work, saving the cook-boy of the 5.s. "Loong Sang" and other persons from vessels drifting down stream.

His Majesty the King cabled a message of sympathy to the Governor in regard to the sad loss of life and the damage to ships and property.

headline: FRANCE DENIES COMMUNIST ASSERTION
text:
(Havas Agency.)

The Ministry of War denies emphatically the assertion of the Communist paper L'Humanité, saying that two French battalions were prepared to fraternise with the Drusés near Rashaya.

headline: REQUEST FOR PEACE
text: It is reported from Beirut that in reply to the request for direct peace negotiations, the High Commissioner told the Jebel Druses that they must first cease hostilities.

headline: KING'S SPEECH.
text:
SOCIALIST DEBATE.

(Hculer'a Seroae.)

London Feb. 4

In the House of Commons, the debate on the Labour amendent to the Address in Reply to the Speech from The Throne, which was moved by Mr. R. Snowden, resolved itself into a discussion on Socialism versus non-Socialism.

Mr. Snowden contended that during the Government's year of office unemployment had increased wages had declined, and profits had risen.

The Labourite, Mr. Johnston, referring to the projected Labour Hours Conference feared that the Washington Convention itself was destroyed by the Conference excluding India, China, and Japan; he emphasised the long hours and inferior conditions in Japan. Sir John Simon (Liberal), in opposing the amendment, asked how the coal industry find makets under public control which was lacking under private ownership? Sir A. Steel-Maitland, replying, denied that the situation had become worse. Notably there had been an increase in wages, whilst as regards unemployment the Government would welcome the co-operation of all Parties, and was even willing to discuss the establishment of a joint Committee of all Parties.

The debate was adjourned.

headline: "H.K. ELECTRIC."
text:
THOSE NEGOTIATIONS WITH AMOY

TERMS REJECTED.

At the time of a boom in shares of the Hongkong Electric Co., Ltd., about a year or so ago, a rumour was current that the company would benefit considerably by a concession in the foreign settlement of Kulangsu, Amoy.

Light. is now thrown on the matter by the “China Mail’s correspondent who reports the annual meeting of ratepayers.

headline: TENDERS STILL WANTED.
text:
For many months the question of ways and means of providing better electric light in the Settlement has been at issue. Reporting upon the matter, the Chairman of the Council said: "The electric light supply has, if anything, deteriorated and residents have to depend to a great extent on other means of lighting." “In the meantime the efforts taken to obtain an improved service have proved abortive, but it is imperative that definite and decisive action be taken without further loss of time. The resolution unanimously adopted by the ratepayers at a special meeting held on September 19, 1924, authorising the Council to take steps to terminate the existing agreement, and to proceed to open negotiations with the Hongkong Electric Co., Ltd., resulted in a draft agreement being drawn up. This agreement was submitted to the ratepayers at a special meeting held on July 31, 1925, but was rejected. A committee of the Council is making investigations as to the most suitable method of solving the electric light question.”

After considerable discussion at the annual meeting on January 29, the following resolution was passed:

"Resolved: That the incoming Council call for tenders for the erection of an electric light and power plant on Kulangsu, and ask for particulars as to alternating current or direct current, or other similar terms, as they may decide, and submit said tenders to the ratepayers as soon as possible."

headline: CANTON'S BOYCOTT. / STATEMENT IN HOUSE OF
text:
WHY NEGOTIATIONS FAILED.

An important statement in regard to the anti-British strike and boycott in Canton was made in the House of Commons by Sir Austen Chamberlain, who referred to the recent negotiations for a settlement; expressed his admiration for the resource and courage of the British communities of Hongkong, Canton, and Swatow; explained why it is not advisable to despatch a Special Commissioner to Canton; and asserted that he was still giving the whole question his closest consideration.

headline: SINISTER INFLUENCES.
text:
Sir Austen Chamberlain, Foreign Secretary, made a statement on the situation in China in the House of Commons today. He said that His Majesty's Government was giving careful and constant attention to the serious problem arising out of the anti-British strike and boycott in Southern China. At the beginning of the year it seemed likely that the negotiations between Hongkong and Canton would be successful. They had, unfortunately, broken down in a manner which must make it clear to the rest of China and, indeed, to the whole world that the Government of Canton was for the time being under influences so blindly anti-British that they were not open to reasonable settlement.

Our Friendly Policy. The position in the rest of China was different. The policy of the British Government, having been dictated by a sincere desire to promote friendly relations with the Chinese people, and being inspired by their legitimate aspirations, this attitude of patience and conciliation was bearing fruit in the slow but steady restoration of friendship and good will between the British and Chinese peoples. The trade conditions in the Yangtse Valley were now improving, and would be equally improving in North China if it were not for civil war, whilst order was being re-established.

There were many signs that these lawless actions were directly attributable to Communistic activities, which had disgusted all sections of the Chinese people, who were very far from approving the actions of the extremist section in Canton. This, feeling would doubtless spread, unless the intervention of the foreign Powers strengthened the extremists and thus united China against the aggressives.

Hongkong Prised. “Meanwhile,” Sir Austen Chamberlain continued, “I must be allowed to express my admiration for the resource and courage with which the British Colony of Hongkong and the British communities of Canton and Swatow have faced so serious a situation. The whole question has recently been examined and now and most carefully by the Foreign Office in conjunction with our representatives in China, and I shall continue to give it my closest attention.”

headline: MEXICAN LAWS.
text:
BRITISH MINISTER LODGES PROTEST.

TO AMERICAN

SIMILAR

Washington, Feb. 10. It is understood that Mr. Esmond Ovey, the British Minister to Mexico, has lodged a formal protest with the Mexican Foreign Office against the anti-allen Land and Petroleum Labs. The protest, it is reported, is substantially in line with that made by the United States. ing in Canton, any good purpose would be served in sending a Special Commissioner to confer with the Canton Government and de facto Governments in South China with the object of impressing upon them the necessity of terminating the situation.

The despatch of such a Commissioner would only serve to undermine the authority of the British representative, which was in most competent hands. It was also unlikely to remedy the weakness of the Central Government in Peking.

Sir Austen Chamberlain asked notice to be given of the question whether there is any relaxation of the ostracism of British firms by other foreign firms who are afraid of losing their servants if they have intercourse with them.

Replying to a supplementary question Sir Austen Chamberlain said that one of the greatest difficulties in the situation was the weakness of the Central Government in Peking.

Replying to Mr. F. W. Pethick-Lawrence (Labour, Leicester), Sir Austen Chamberlain, after referring to the Chinese authorities' refusal to accept the cheque for compensation in respect of the incidents in Shanghai last May, said he hoped that the policy of patient conciliation, steadily followed by the British Government, was tending gradually to remove the ill-feeling caused by those incidents and to restore good will between the British and Chinese peoples. He added that he did not regret that the matter was referred to a judicial authority, which had substantiated our decision to make the facts known.

Replying to Commander John Kenworthy (Liberal, Hull Central), Sir Austen Chamberlain said he had no official information as to whether any Britons were serving in Chan Kwingming's army. He referred the questioner to Article 75 of the China Order in Council, 1925 regarding participation on either side which, he said, was being strictly enforced.

headline: BOXER INDEMNITY. / CHINESE MEMBERS OF THE COMMITTEE
text:
NAMES AWAITED.

In the House of Commons, replying to the Hon. C. P. Trevelyan (Labour, Newcastle-on-Tyne), Sir Austen Chamberlain stated that after consultation with the British members of the Committee established under the China Indemnity Act, 1925, the British representatives in China, and the Chinese Foreign Minister, he (Sir A. Chamberlain) had approached three eminent Chinese to join the Committee. Their names would be published as soon as they definitely accepted.

headline: CONTEMPT OF COURT. / ACTIVITIES WHICH HINDERED THE LAW.
text:
TINY DEFENDANTS:

The activities of the white ants who have dared to interfere with the smooth working of the administration of justice in the Supreme Court are to be effectively checked.

For some months the three huge circles of electric bulbs suspended from the ceiling have given a certain amount of trouble. It has only needed the vibration from a passing tram or car, or a passer by in the corridor, for them so far to forget themselves as to wink simultaneously.

For such contempt of court they were marked down for attention but it has not hitherto been possible to get on which the work owing to pressure of court work. As the Supreme Court has now no sitting until the 22nd., advantage being taken of the interval, scaffolding having been erected in the court and a dozen or more workmen are engaged in the work.

It was discovered that the industry of the white ants had led to the inconvenience to which the court was put, an important connection having been rendered imperfect and inoperative when subject to vibration.

A Government ambulance was damaged when it collided with a tram car at Des Vœux Road yesterday.

Calendars advertising the well known products of Meera. Cadbury Bros., Ltd. of Bourneville and Messrs. J. S. Fry and Sons, Ltd., of Bristol have been received from John D. Hutchison and Co. who are the agents for these chocolate manufacturers. Cadbury's depicts a Chinese maiden of rank being attended by her maids and Fry's two young Chinese girls who recommend the products.

TODAY'S DOLLAR The closing rate of the dollar, on demand, to day was 2/4 7/16.

headline: WIRELESS DISPUTE.
text:
MEETING OF BOTH PARTIES ARRANGED.

MINISTER'S EFFORT

It was announced in the House of Commons that the Minister of Labour (Sir A. H. Steel-Maitland) had arranged a meeting of the two parties in the marine wireless dispute to take place at the Ministry of Labour this afternoon. The Minister said that he awited the results of that meeting before taking further action.

A motor car driven by the Hon Mr. D. W. Treeman was slightly damaged in a collision with a tram car near the Naval Yard yesterday. Robbery is thought to be the motive for the suspected murder of the proprietor of an oil shop at Nam Tung Street, Shamshuipo, on Tuesday night. The body bore marks of strangulation. An employee of the shop is reported to be missing.

headline: CAFE INCIDENT.
text:
EUROPEAN ATTACKED WITH A KNIFE.

WAITER CONVICTED

Evidence was taken by Major C. Willson at the Central Magistracy this morning in a charge of assault preferred against a Chinese waiter of the Victoria Café, Des Voux Rond Central.

The complainant, Mr James Royston Stuart said that some dirty knives and forks were placed on the table when he went to have tillin along with his wife on Tuesday. Defendant took offences at a request to bring clean knives and attacked him with a knife in his hand. Complainant struck in self-defence and received a cut in his thumb.

Defendant pleaded that he misunderstood what was wanted and on asking complainant to repeat the order he was struck in the face. Complainant then tried to hit him with a flower pot. He denied attacking complainant with a knife. A witness called by defendant stated that he was in the inner room and saw the complainant pushing the defendant away. Defendant demonstrated and was struck in the cheek. Witness took a knife away from defendant's hand, and there was a clamour by the waiters for complainant's arrest.

Defendant explained that the complainant attempted to get away without paying for his meal.

Complainant's wife stated in evidence that she did not actually see defendant pick up a knife nor did she see her husband strike defendant. The Magistrate held that the charge had been proved and sentenced defendant to one month's hard labour.

headline: No. 19,727 HONGKONG, TUESDAY, FEBRUARY 16, 1926. / MR. D. K. BLAIR'S DEATH.
text:
His War, Strike And Sport Work.

The death is announced in a brief cable which gives no details. of Mr. D. K. Blair, late Secretary of the Hongkong Chamber of Commerce. Death took place yesterday.

A studio portrait of Mr. D. K. Blair, taken shortly before his departure for Home, after many years' residence in the Colony

Whilst it will be a matter of grief to his many friends in Hong- kong, to those who saw Mr. Blair at Home in the summer of last year, the news will not come as a great shock.

Mr. Blair left Hongkong early in April, 1924. He had been in indifferent health and it was on medical advice that he left for Home.

He had served the Colony for many years and in different spheres and his judgment, discretion and long acquaintance with local conditions enabled him to fill with credit the responsible post he held when he left the Colony.

For his excellent work on behalf of the Colony, the late Mr. Blair was presented by the Government with a silver salver engraved with the Colony's emblem "as an indication of the appreciation of the Government of Hongkong of the services you have so willingly given on various occasions."

A sum of money was also voted to Mr. Blair by the Chamber of Commerce in order that he might purchase some memento as a mark of appreciation of his services.

When the Peak Hospital was handed over to the Government, Mr. Blair was appointed honorary secretary and treasurer. Mr. Blair reorganised the Hospital with such success that the Government was moved to express its warmest thanks "for" the very creditable manner" in which he "voluntarily carried out the arduous work." He also received a letter from the Colonial Treasurer expressing his sincere gratitude for all he had done, "in putting the Peak Hospital on a satisfactory basis both as regards efficiency and business matters."

Apart from his official work, Mr. Blair was best known as the Honorary Secretary of the St. Andrew's Society. The following tribute was paid to him by that Society on the occasion of his departure:—“As Secretary of the Society, you have placed the organisation at a high water mark of efficiency, and your personal interest and able management have been outstanding features in our Scottish celebrations.” Mr. Blair was a keen mason, being deputy master of Lodge Eastern Scotia, Number 923, of which he was also for many years a past master. His impending departure brought him a letter of sincere appreciation for his “many services and unequalled generosity;” and the lodge also presented him with suitably inscribed emblems of the craft as a souvenir.

headline: China One Jiail
text:
ESTABLISHED

Government And Shameen

Although, owing to certain factors, the directors of the Hongkong, Canton, and Macao Steamboat Co., Ltd, announce no dividend for the year, a sound position as regards the balance sheet and working generally was disclosed at the annual meeting this morning.

The Chairman, the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak, in the course of his statement, said that he had reason to believe that the Company would receive financial support from the Government in meeting the loss involved in keeping up communication between Hongkong and Shameen.

The following were present:—The Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak (Chairman), the Hon. Mr. A. O. Lang, Messrs. W. E. Clarke, T. G. Weall, J. M. Alves, H. Staples Smith, and R. M. Austin (Directors), Mr. John Arnold (Secretary), also the following shareholders:—Messrs. S. H. Michael, L. S. Greenhill, Cheng Ching-po, S. Danenberg, J. Owen Hughes, Paul Lauder, G. E. Townes, and Geo. S. Zimmern.

During his residence in Hongkong, Mr. Blair took the keenest interest in yachting and together with Mr. Frank Smyth his name will long be remembered as prominently associated with the progress of the Royal Hongkong Yacht Club. For many years Mr. Blair was Sailing Secretary and he did splendid work in connection with the Club's annual regattas. It was in recognition of his hard work as an official of that Club that he was made Vice-Commodore and later Commodore, which position he held at the time of his departure from the Colony.

Before he left, Mr. Blair was the recipient of a handsome solid silver cigar and cigarette box, the gift of prominent members of the Yacht Club whose signatures were inscribed on it.

Mr. Blair was a native of Irvine, Ayrshire. He first came to the East in 1889 and was originally in the service of the Eastern Extension Telegraph Company serving Shanghai and North China as well as Hongkong. During the Boxer rebellion he was in the North and helped to maintain telegraph services at Tientsin and Taku forts during those hazardous times.

The late Mr. Blair came to Hongkong as Assistant Secretary of the Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce. Having acted as Secretary on numerous occasions, he was appointed Secretary in 1921.

Mr. Blair was a Justice of the Peace for Hongkong

During the Seamen's Strike, tribute was paid by the Government to Mr. Blair's excellent work "which had been of the greatest assistance" in conducting to the smooth running of the services.

Another branch of his earlier activities was that in connection with the raising of a Signalling Section of the Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps during the War when he trained many residents in the art of telegraphic signalling. He remained with his section until it was desbanded.

Much sympathy will be felt with the late Mr. Blair's family. TO-DAY'S MEETING

you will, I am sure, realise that it is difficult "and indeed would be unwise for me to dwell at length on the incidents of the past seven months which are common knowledge to you all." Under all the circumstances, the balance sheet may be considered satisfactory. For the first six months of the year, our trading results compared very favourably with the average figures of preceding years and given normal times we feel certain we could have set before you a good balance sheet. The year has been marked by the strike in June and the subsequent boycott of British shipping in South China. Our Macao service was suspended from June 18 to July 27 when one boat was put on the run. Less than a month later, August 22, the full service to Macao was resumed. In September, at the request of the authorities, and in the consultation with the Government, the "Honam" re-opened the Canton sailing and we have maintained our Cantonsailings continuously ever since. It was obvious that the boats could not earn a profit but it was felt by your directors that it was in the interests of all to maintain communication with Shameen and Canton and our flag upon the river. I have reason to believe that we shall receive financial support from the Government in meeting the loss which has been involved in giving vital and essential service, which is not likely to be forgotten by our loyal supporters, Chinese as well as foreign, when times are once more normal and our fleet is in full operation. It is fitting here that I should record the high appreciation of your directors of the services of the floating staff under especially the trying conditions which have prevailed. I may say that on re-starting the Canton service with the "Honam" and when satisfactory insurance on the lives of the officers and crew had not yet been completed, to a man, from the Captain downwards, the officers volunteered to sail with

Our fleet has been added to since last we met by the new "Taishan," which promises to be the most popular boat on the river, as she will unquestionably be the most beautiful and best equipped.

Running but of the verandah of a house at Kowloon City Road, a Chinese was knocked down by a sanitary waggon and received a broken arm.

In alighting from a tram car while in motion, a Chinese youth received injuries to his head. He is now lying in a critical condition at the hospital.

headline: CITY BURGLARY
text:
AUBERT CAFE THE LATEST VICTIM.

$1,500 LOOT TAKEN

Thieves Help Themselves

to food.

A haul of $500 in money and property valued at $1,000 was taken by burglars from the Albert Cafe in Queen's Road Central after the establishment had closed at about midnight on Monday. In addition the thieves helped themselves liberally to roast fowl milk, and the other French delicacies with which the Cafe is stocked.

Marks of the gang's work during the night were apparent in the disarranged condition of the contents of the glass cases when the proprietor, M. Albert Guetat, opened the main door from the outside yesterday morning.

The thieves slid down some bamboo scaffolding running the full length of the wall of the two-stoneyed building at the rear and over the flat roof of the kitchen. A ladder placed here helped them to alight in the yard outside the kitchen. A thin wire netting barrier placed over the iron barred windows of the kitchen was cut through and the gang got through this hole into the kitchen which gave them free access to the premises.

The money was taken by breaking open the drawers of a wooden table used by the proprietor's wife as a cash desk. Two mall leather cases containing passports, the Cafe licence and other documents were also taken from the drawers, but the lady's marriage licence was fortunately left behind. Property stolen comprised silver crockery articles, an electric iron, a weighing balance, linen and other goods.

The door leading into the lavatory from the yard was also forced open. Another door from this room gives access to the alley way between the Cafe and the Asiatic Building. This door was found locked from the inside when the theft was discovered in the morning, but it is not unlikely that the stolen property or a part of it was passed on to a confederate outside.

As in the majority of city burglaries, the gang possessed an intimate knowledge of the building and its contents and took everything of value which they could conveniently carry away with them. Suspicion rests with several coolies, who were in the employment of the Cafe and had to be discharged recently.

A report of the theft was made to the police yesterday, but so far no arrests have resulted.

headline: STRIKE IN BURMA.
text:
OILFIELD LABOURERS "DOWN TOOLS"

THREE DEMANDS MADE

(Reuler's Serifoe.)

Two-thirds of the oilfield labourers of the Burma Oil Company at Yenangyaung and Chauk Singu are involved in a strike demanding a reduction of taxation, the abolition of the Labour Bureau, and the adoption of a monthly wage arrangement instead of a daily one.

headline: SOMEWHAT UNIQUE
text:
The annual power and vegetable show of the Hongkong Horticultural Society this year will be somewhat of a unique event. The absence of gardeners for a considerable period was most marked at the Peak, the tremendous growth of grass on the lawns of the Peak Club giving an idea of what things were like for a time. There is thus more scope this year for those who personally attended to their gardens and who have had little chance in previous years of competing against exhibitors who have had several gardeners in constant attendance. Mr. T. E. Pearce is said to have taken a keen interest in attending to his garden and although it is early to prophesy, he should be in a position to place some excel

Lower level gardens were less affected by the absence of workers than were those on the Peak and Chinese exhibitors' should be in a strong position in this respect. Seen this morning by a “China Mail” representative, Mr. E. B. C. Hornell, ‘the Honorary Secretary of the Society’ said that it was impossible at present to forecast the number of entries or their standard but it was hoped that the show would be as successful as ever. They were hoping that the prize for competitors who had not won before would lead many to compete who had not yet done so.

headline: CANTON SHIPPING
text:
DRASTIC ACTION BY THE CUSTOMS

FORTIRTIALLY CLOSED

The most important development in Canton for some time is reported by the decision of the Commissioner of the Chinese Maritime Customs not to issue—as from to-day—any permits for the loading or unloading of cargo.

As the natural result of this decision the steamer "Lung Shan" belonging to the Hongkong, Canton, and Macao Steamboat Co., Limited, did not leave on the usual voyage to Canton this morning. It is, of course, quite useless for cargo to be sent to Canton and only have to be brought back again. Therefore, it follows that other steamers on the run will be affected in the same manner.

It has been common knowledge for a considerable time that the strikers in Canton were interfering illegitimately with the proper functioning of the Maritime Customs. Little or no control could be maintained by the Customs over contraband, and in other ways the Customs' duties were being impeded or dislocated. Eventually matters went from bad to worse, which led the Commissioner of Customs to intimate, through the usual official channels—the Canton Government—that further interference by the strikers with the functioning of the Customs would lead to the Customs taking the drastic action of refusing to grant permits for loading or unloading cargo in the Canton river. This was ignored, and as the interference was persisted in, it was decided to give effect to the threat as from to day.

The Commissioner of Customs, it should be almost needless to point out, acts directly under the control of the Inspector-General of the Chinese Maritime Custom in Peking. It is logical to assume, therefore, that the Commissioner's decision was made with the full approval of the Inspector-General. This fact is worthy of mention inasmuch as it narrows the issue down to a dispute between the Chinese Maritime Customs on the one hand and the Canton Government and/or the strikers on the other. The position is one of extreme importance and gravity, and any further developments will be awaited with considerable inter-

headline: State of Blockade
text:
From the best informed sources it is learned that cargo belonging to nationalists of five Powers had been seized by armed boycott pickets. This cargo was taken prior to examination by the Customs staff, and when in the custody of the Customs. Accordingly, an ultimatum was presented that if the cargo was not returned, action would be taken to secure the revenues of the Customs, such action being to refuse papers for the clearance of ships at Canton and the port of Whampoa.

When a similar incident occurred toward the end of 1923 eighteen gunboats of foreign Powers assembled at Canton, to guard the Customs and safeguard the revenue (on the surplus of which foreign loans are secured). Chinese merchants in Hongkong, with connections in Canton, have had little or no news about the developments.

Virtually Canton and Whampoa are now in a state of blockade, as ships will not be able to get through without permission from the Customs.

At present the only ship on the run between Hongkong and Canton, besides the "Lungshan," is the China Navigation Co.'s "Fatshan."

headline: OBITUARY.
text:
It is with sincere regret that the "China Mail" records the death last night of Mr. William Josiah Wilkinson, a Government pensioner and ex-serviceman who is best known as overseer to the Hong-kong Land Investment & Agency Co., Ltd.

Mr. Wilkinson was 55 years of age. Apparently in good health, he went to Macao yesterday for a trip. On his return he complained

of feeling, unwell, and had just taken off his shoes when he fell back and died twenty minutes later.

The deceased gentleman was very popular in the Colony. "Joining the Royal Marines in 1888, he purchased his discharge in Hong Kong in 1894 and joined the Prison Department, retiring on pension (as Principal Warder) in 1910, when he joined the Land Investment Co.

Much sympathy will go out to the far fly. They're avement. Mr. Wilmington is succeeded by his wide, seven sons, four daughters, and fourteen grandchildren. His eldest son Willie and his daughter Voilet are on their way out from Home after a holiday.

headline: CANTON. PIECEGOODS.
text:
A report has reached Hongkong that employees of piecegoods merchants in Canton have been on strike for some days, a dispute starting before China New Year.

The employees have presented a number of terms which now form the subject of negotiation. A conciliatory meeting was to have been held but over a hundred strike pickets attended as spectators. One result was that the merchants left the projected meeting before any discussion was made possible.

The demands all relate to matters of employment and the majority concern the steps (which the men desire) to be taken on dismissal.

headline: DON'T INTERFERE. / CRITICISING A CONSTABLES METHODS
text:
EXPRESS RUNNER FINEO.

"You have a perfect right to protest (the proper course is to go to the Police Station and report what you have seen), but you have no right to lay your hands on the constable," said Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning in imposing a fine of $10 on Eric Eugene Roy, runner of the American Express Company, on a charge of obstructing a constable while on duty at Lyndhurst Terrace.

The evidence was that the constable (in plain clothes) arrested an amah for selling chickens and that the defendant interfered and struck him. Denying the allegation of assault, defendant said that he asked the constable not to drag the woman by the hand while she had a child on her back. The amah admitted that the defendant pulled the constable away while the latter was holding her.

headline: SIX MONTHS. / MORRISON HILL FIGHT SEQUEL.
text:
DEATH ONLY ACCELERATED

The earth caplie charged with the manslaughter on January 9 of one of the other coolies working on the demolition of Morrison Hill was sentenced to six months' imprisonment at the Criminal Sessions this morning.

Medical evidence was given to show that the deceased had been ill before the fight which had led to the prisoner's appearance in the dock. Death had been accelerated as a result of the blows he received.

headline: Uhtina / CANTON CUSTOMS
text:
QUESTIONS IN HOUSE OF COMMONS.

FULL STATEMENT DESIRED

In the House of Commons, Lieut.-Colonel Sir Frederick Hall (Conservative, Dulwich) requested an opportunity for the House to have a full statement on the present position in China.

Mr. Stanley Baldwin (Prime Minister) said that there was no material change since the statement made on February 10 by Sir Austen Chamberlain, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs; but he (Mr. Baldwin) did not think that a further statement would serve any useful purpose at present.

Mr. Dennis Herbert (Conservative, Watford), called attention to the report that the Commissioner of Customs had closed the port of Canton, suggesting that "that showed that the people on the spot were doing their best to preserve the interests of British traders."

Mr. Baldwin said that he had seen such statement. He added that there would be an opportunity of questioning the Secretary's State for Foreign Affairs when the latter returned.

Colonel J. C. Wedgwood (Labour, Newcastle-under-Lyme) asked whether the closing of the port of Canton was done after consultation with the Government? Mr. Baldwin said that he required notice to be given of that question.

[[The foregoing] merely demonstrates the ignorance at Home, even amongst members of Parliament, in regard to the facts connected with the decision of the Commissioner of Customs at Canton not to issue permits for loading and unloading cargo. To speak of "those on the spot doing their best to preserve the interests of British trade" shows an entire misconception of the relationship between the Chinese Customs and the Chinese nation. As clearly stated in these columns on Monday the issue at stake has arisen between the Chinese Maritime Customs on the one hand and the Canton Government and/or boycott pickets on the other hand.]]

The Wai-chiao-pu (Chinese Foreign Office) this afternoon telegraphed to the Commissioner of Foreign Affairs at Canton, instructing him to investigate the Customs affair.

headline: No Compliance Yet.
text:
Forty steamers are idle as tn result of the closing of the point

The Canton Government at present does not give any sign of complying with the Customs Commissioner's requirements. The Chinese appear delighted at the check given to the Strike Committee's illegal acts.

Over a dozen piracies of foreign steamers have occurred in the Pearl River in the past few months, the latest being two seizures whilst the vessels were lying anchored at Whampoa, within a few hundred yards of the Military Academy.

text:
Mrs. F. H. Holyonk was able to leave the Peak Hospital yesterday. Although she may still be laid up for some time yet, she is making satisfactory progress.

A house coolie in the employment of Mr. J. Glen, of East Point Terrace, was taken to the Government Civil Hospital yesterday following an attack by a dog. The animal has not been traced.

headline: Other Reports:
text:
Private information to hand is that the Kwangtung Political Council met on Monday to discuss the matter, that Mr. Fu Ping-sheung (Superintendent of Customs and of the Foreign Department) has "been in conversation" with the Customs authorities, and that a request has been made for a resumption pending negotiation. How far these reports are true can only be surmised in the absence of authentic confirmation.

On Monday, (when the closure came into force), the examination office formed jointly by the Boycott, Committee and the merchants was started. As cargo could neither be shipped nor landed there was no work to do. A native piecegoods dealer is said to have transported some cargo along to the temporary shed near the Steamboat Co.'s wharf (which is quite close to the Customs House on the Bund) but the merchandise was not "passed" as the official on duty (appointed by the so-called examination bureau, or prize-court) was absent.

The closure is also said to have taken the Canton merchants by surprise. On Monday morning when it was found that the “customs had been closed” prices of imported commodities went up. Flour rose 30 cents a sack (of 50 lbs.) and sugar about 20 cents a bag, says the Wah Tsz. Yat Po's correspondent.

headline: Trouble to End?
text:
There is more than a possibility that shipping will be admitted into Canton and Whampoa harbours again on Friday.

From a very good source it is gathered that steps are being taken which will result in the former position being restored. How this is to be accomplished has not been divulged. One surmise is that the request of the Canton Customs (for the return of cargo belonging to nationals of five Powers, seized by armed boycott pickets) will be complied with. Although there is nothing definite firms interested are making quiet moves in preparation for the re-opening of the port.

Story About Leather. From the same source it was learned that the seizure by pickets of a large quantity (said to be about 200 bales) of foreign leather was one of the last acts which caused the decision of the Commissioner of Customs to be reached.

The story goes that on arrival (either at Canton or Whampoa) from abroad, that part of each piece of high-class leather bearing the factory's stamp was cut off, and the lot then seized without going through the Customs and paying duty.

Mails To Shameen. With the cessation in the river traffic, the postal service is being maintained by train. Mr. J. W. Faulkner, insulation engineer, said that the defendant had no authority to take the lubing which was part of the material issued for a contract at the Hongkong Club.

headline: Jutail / THREE ACCIDENTS.
text:
TWO HOSPITAL CASES

The sudden stoppage of a motor lorry at Queen's Road East, without giving a signal it is alleged, led to a motor cycle travelling behind crashing into the vehicle yester-day.

A Chinese lady seated in the side car of the machine was thrown out and injured, but she refused to go to hospital.

A motor car coming out of Wing Lok Street into Des Vaux Road West ran into an empty ricsha and overturned it. The ricsha coolie received severe injuries which necessitated his removal to hospital.

Another hospital case was provided in an accident at Queen's Road East. A Chinese youth ran out from a verandah and was struck down by a motor car. He was injured in the head.

headline: LOAN TO ITALY.
text:
AMERICAN BANKERS' BIG DEAL

New York, Feb. 23. Negotiations have been completed by American bankers for a loan of twenty million dollars to the Italian Public Utilities Credit Institute.

This is the first external transaction arranged by the Institute. It is notified that the draw for the Derby sweepstakes will take place at the Civil Service Cricket Club on Monday next at 6 p.m. Tickets not paid for before the draw will be cancelled.

headline: NOVEL BILL. / SAFEGUARDING NATIONAL TREASURES
text:
A BAN ON EXPORT..

The House of Commons to-day passed the first reading of a private Bill introduced by Sir Henry Sligger, Solicitor General in the late Labour Government, prohibiting the export of works of art and ancient or historic buildings and monuments.

In introducing the Bill Sir H. Slesser pointed out that persons of great wealth abroad had paid the compliment to Great Britain of paying great prices for her national possessions. "Enumerating types of national treasures recently taken out of this country, he mentioned Priory House, Warwick, a beautiful old building which had been totally removed, and which, he believed, was to be or had been actually re-erected in the United States. There was, he said, a constant flow of some of the most beautiful British works of art to America." Historical records and ancient books, which were an absolutely invaluable heritage for the understanding of the history of this country, were becoming the subject of traffic by antique dealers, and were being sold to the highest bidder.

headline: China the Initial / ACCIDENTS.
text:
MOTOR BOAT SUNK.

· A series of motor accidents yesterday ended with a harbour collision this morning.

The first of the accidents occurred in the morning near the Central Market when a Chinese boy ran in front of a motor car driven by Dr. B. A. Tottenham, of the University. The boy was slightly injured.

A coolie running out of the Sang Lee matshed at Praya East went under a motor cycle driven by Mr. A. May. The man received some bruises.

A private owned car was wrecked by losing control in Garden Road. Two small boys were injured. Opposite the Mongkok Police Station, a Kai Tack motor bus had the worst of a collision with another vehicle.
